# Anomaly Label Criteria: SMHI Warning System Grounding

## Overview

The V9 anomaly detection head uses **3-class severity labels** grounded in the official
SMHI Class I/II/III heavy snowfall warning criteria documented in:

> Yang, W., Olsson, J., Andersson, J.C.M., et al. (2023). *Spatio-temporal
> characterization of warnings and advisories issued by SMHI 2011–2020 with focus on
> multiple hydrological hazards.* SMHI Hydrology No. 23.
> Report file: `RH23_Spatio-temporal_characterization_of_warnings...2011-2020.pdf`

These criteria were in effect **until October 26, 2021**, when SMHI transitioned to an
impact-based Yellow/Orange/Red system. Our label scheme uses the physical Class I/II/III
thresholds throughout 2015–2024 because:
1. They are publicly documented and reproducible.
2. They are physically interpretable (absolute meteorological thresholds).
3. The post-2021 Yellow/Orange/Red thresholds are regionally adapted and not publicly available.

---

## SMHI Class I/II/III Heavy Snowfall Criteria (Table 1, RH23)

| Class | Criterion | Approximate Snow Depth Change |
|-------|-----------|-------------------------------|
| Class I | >5 mm/6h snowfall equivalent | ~5 cm/6h → 10–20 cm/day |
| Class II | >20 mm/12h **OR** >12 mm/12h + wind >8 m/s | ~10–40 cm/day or compound |
| Class III | >35 mm/12h **OR** >25 mm/12h + wind >8 m/s | ~17–70 cm/day or compound |

Note: mm values are liquid-equivalent precipitation. Converted to snow depth assuming
~10:1 snow density ratio (standard operational assumption). The wind threshold of
**8 m/s** is the exact SMHI criterion for compound wind-snow Class II/III warnings.

---

## Label Definitions (V9 — `_create_anomaly_labels`)

### Label 0: Normal
No SMHI-warning-equivalent event. Routine snow conditions.

### Label 1: Serious (Class I equivalent)
Notable snowfall that may require attention but is generally manageable.

| Rule | Criterion | SMHI Basis |
|------|-----------|------------|
| Moderate accumulation | 5 cm < snow_change ≤ 10 cm/day | Class I depth-change range |
| Persistent accumulation | snow_change > 5 cm/day for 3 consecutive days | Sustained Class I loading |

### Label 2: Extreme (Class II/III equivalent)
Dangerous conditions requiring active warning. **Overrides Label 1**.

| Rule | Criterion | SMHI Basis |
|------|-----------|------------|
| Heavy accumulation | snow_change > 10 cm/day | Class II+ depth-change threshold |
| Heavy frozen precip | frozen_precip > 5 cm/day (MESAN `frsn1h`) | Class II+ direct measurement |
| Wind-snow compound | snow_change > 5 cm/day AND wind_speed > 8 m/s | Class II compound (exact threshold) |
| Rapid melt | snow_change < −5 cm/day for 3 consecutive days | Class I+ high river flow risk |
| Rain-on-snow | precip > 5mm AND temp > 0°C AND snow > 10 cm | Pluvial+fluvial compound flood risk |

**Priority rule**: Label 2 always takes precedence. If any Label 2 condition is satisfied,
the sample is labeled 2 regardless of Label 1 criteria.

---

## Unit Clarification: `frozen_precip`

The MESAN variable `frozen_precip` is the `frsn1h` parameter (frozen precipitation,
hourly) summed to 24-hour totals. **Units are millimetres of liquid-equivalent**,
which the preprocessor stores in cm-equivalent snow depth using a 1:1 approximation
for the frozen precip column. When comparing against SMHI snowfall thresholds
(mm/12h in RH23 Table 1), the threshold of 5 cm/day in our code corresponds to
approximately 10 mm liquid-equivalent per 12 hours — close to the SMHI Class II
lower bound of 12 mm/12h. This is a conservative approximation; the wind-snow
compound rule (`wind_speed > 8 m/s`) captures additional Class II events at lower
precipitation rates.

---

## Post-2021 System Change

SMHI introduced an impact-based warning system on **October 26, 2021**, replacing
the physical Class I/II/III thresholds with regionally adapted Yellow/Orange/Red
severity levels. Key distinctions:

| Aspect | Pre-2021 (Class I/II/III) | Post-2021 (Yellow/Orange/Red) |
|--------|--------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Basis | Physical thresholds (mm, cm, m/s) | Impact-based (consequence-driven) |
| Documentation | Publicly available (Table 1, RH23) | Regionally adapted, not public |
| Spatial variation | Uniform national thresholds | Region-specific thresholds |
| Our model coverage | 2015–2024 (crosses the boundary) | Not reproducible from public data |

**Our approach**: We apply the pre-2021 physical Class I/II/III thresholds uniformly
throughout 2015–2024. This ensures reproducibility and physical interpretability at
the cost of some label noise in 2022–2024 (where SMHI's operational thresholds may
differ slightly from ours).

**Critical note**: Class I ≠ Yellow, Class II ≠ Orange. The post-2021 impact-based
system is not a direct mapping from the pre-2021 physical classes. We do not claim
our labels correspond to any specific post-2021 warning color.

---

## Expected Label Distribution

Based on SMHI warning statistics (RH23, Table 3) and station-level analysis:

| Label | Description | Expected Prevalence |
|-------|-------------|---------------------|
| 0 | Normal | ~88–90% |
| 1 | Serious (Class I) | ~6–8% |
| 2 | Extreme (Class II/III) | ~2–4% |

This distribution informs the CrossEntropyLoss class weights in V9:
- `w0 = 1.0` (Normal — baseline)
- `w1 = 12.0` ≈ 89/7 (Serious — inverse frequency)
- `w2 = 22.0` ≈ 89/4 (Extreme — inverse frequency)

---

## Why Multi-Class vs Binary?

The V7b/V8 binary approach (anomaly = 1 if any extreme event) has two limitations:

1. **Severity conflation**: A 6 cm/day snowfall (serious but manageable) receives the
   same label as a 30 cm/day blizzard with 15 m/s winds. The model cannot distinguish
   nuance in the label signal.

2. **Threshold mismatch**: V7b used `snow_change > 20 cm/day` as the primary rule,
   capturing only Class III+ events. Class I and Class II events (comprising the majority
   of SMHI warnings) were entirely missed.

The 3-class scheme captures the full SMHI warning hierarchy and provides more informative
training signal for the shared encoder, which must learn to distinguish normal conditions,
serious-but-manageable events, and truly dangerous situations.

---

## Citation

Yang, W., Olsson, J., Andersson, J.C.M., Lam Hung, V., Sörensen, J., Olofsson, M.,
Sjökvist, E., and Gustafsson, D. (2023). Spatio-temporal characterization of warnings
and advisories issued by SMHI 2011–2020 with focus on multiple hydrological hazards.
SMHI Hydrology Report No. 23. Norrköping, Sweden.

# Problem Statement & Research Questions

## 1. Problem Definition

### The Core Challenge
Nordic snow dynamics are governed by identical physical processes whether predicting:
- **Spatial variation**: How does snow depth differ across locations?
- **Temporal evolution**: How will snow depth change over the next week?
- **Extreme events**: When will dangerous rapid changes occur?

Current approaches treat these as separate problems with separate models, losing information about shared underlying physics.

### Why This Matters
Snow is critical for:
- **Hydropower production** (Sweden: ~45% electricity from hydropower; depends on spring snowmelt)
- **Water resource management** (predict streamflow, plan reservoirs)
- **Flood risk** (rapid melt or rain-on-snow events)
- **Avalanche forecasting** (emergency response)
- **Climate monitoring** (indicator of climate change)

**Current limitations**:
1. SMHI station network is spatially sparse — only ~100-120 stations with comprehensive weather data across all of Sweden
2. Snow depth predictions are often based on simple statistical or physics-based models
3. Extreme event warnings rely on manual expert judgment and threshold-based rules
4. No unified framework integrating spatial prediction, temporal forecasting, and anomaly detection

### The Opportunity
Deep learning can learn complex non-linear relationships from data that statistical models miss:
- Temperature + wind + humidity → melt rate (non-linear)
- Recent precipitation patterns → avalanche risk (complex)
- Seasonal + geographic context → accurate predictions everywhere

---

## 2. Research Questions

### Primary Research Question
> **Can a single multi-task deep learning model learn unified representations of snow physics that enable superior performance on spatial interpolation, temporal forecasting, and anomaly detection tasks compared to single-task models?**

### Secondary Research Questions

#### Question 2A (Spatial Interpolation)
> How can we predict snow depth at unobserved locations using only weather observations and geographic context? What geographic features are most important?

**Hypothesis**: Models informed by elevation, latitude, and land cover will better generalize across regions.

#### Question 2B (Temporal Forecasting)
> Can we forecast snow depth 7 days ahead with skill > 0.5 (compared to climatology)? Does skill vary by season?

**Hypothesis**: Winter forecasts more skillful (larger snow signal), spring forecasts harder (complex melt dynamics).

#### Question 2C (Anomaly Detection)
> Can we predict extreme snow events (>50cm/day, rapid melt >5cm/day for 5+ days) with recall > 70% and false alarm rate < 30%?

**Hypothesis**: Model will capture precursory signals in weather/snow patterns that predict extremes.

#### Question 2D (Multi-Task Learning)
> Does multi-task learning improve performance on individual tasks compared to single-task baselines?

**Hypothesis**: Shared encoder learns robust representations of snow physics; tasks benefit from each other.

---

## 3. Data Overview

The project uses a **hybrid data approach** combining two complementary sources: MESAN gridded analysis for meteorological features and SMHI station observations for ground-truth snow depth.

### MESAN Gridded Analysis (Input Features)
**Source**: SMHI Grid Archive (opendata-download-grid-archive.smhi.se)
**Type**: Gridded reanalysis product combining station data, radar, satellite, and NWP models
**Spatial Resolution**: 2.5 km grid (dense, spatially complete coverage of Sweden)
**Temporal Resolution**: Hourly (aggregated to daily for this project)
**Temporal Coverage**: 2015-2024 (10 winters, October-April)
**Data Format**: GRIB files (one per day at 06:00 UTC analysis time)

**Variables extracted** (11 from GRIB, 2 derived, 1 from metadata):
- Temperature (2m), precipitation (24h), wind speed (10m, from u/v components)
- Humidity (2m), frozen precipitation (24h), visibility, cloud cover
- Ground temperature, wind gust, precipitation type/sort (available but not all used in model)
- Cyclical day encoding (day_sin, day_cos) — derived
- Latitude, elevation — from station metadata

**Key characteristics**:
- Spatially complete — no gaps between stations
- Rich physical feature set (~30 variables available)
- Indirect measurements (model analysis, not direct observation)
- Rotated lat/lon grid requiring nearest-neighbor spatial matching

### SMHI Station Snow Depth (Ground Truth)
**Source**: SMHI Open Data API (parameter 8 = Snödjup)
**Type**: In-situ point measurements
**Spatial Coverage**: 659 stations with snow depth data across Sweden (424 retained after quality filtering)
**Temporal Coverage**: 2015-2024
**Temporal Resolution**: Daily (06:00 UTC)
**Data Format**: CSV via API

**Key characteristics**:
- High-quality ground truth (quality-controlled by SMHI)
- Spatially sparse (point measurements, not gridded)
- Latitude range: 55.3-68.9°N, elevation: -1 to 1220 m
- Prone to missing data (~5-20% per station)

### Data Fusion Strategy
```
MESAN GRIB (2.5 km, ~30 variables)
       ↓ extract nearest grid cell at each station (lat, lon)
Daily feature vectors (20 columns × 1,896 stations × 2,035 days)
       ↓ left-join on (station_id, date)
Station snow depth observations (659 stations)
       ↓ filter ≥70% winter coverage, interpolate ≤3-day gaps
Training data: 783,879 rows × 21 columns × 424 stations
       ↓ per-station 30-day sequences
Input: (N, 30, 12)  Targets: A(N,), B(N,7), D(N,)
```

**Rationale**: Only ~20% of SMHI snow stations also measure the meteorological variables needed for ML training. MESAN solves this by providing spatially complete meteorological coverage at every station location, while station snow depth serves as the ground truth target.

---

## 4. Methodological Approach

### High-Level Strategy
```
1. Download MESAN GRIB data + SMHI station snow depth
   ↓
2. Build data pipeline (MESAN extraction → merge → sequences)
   ↓
3. Design multi-task architecture (shared encoder + 3 heads)
   ↓
4. Implement encoder + three prediction heads
   ↓
5. Train multi-task model, iterate on hyperparameters
   ↓
6. Train single-task baselines for comparison
   ↓
7. Comprehensive evaluation on held-out test year (2024)
   ↓
8. Analysis & visualization
   ↓
9. Write manuscript & submission
```

### Core Innovation
**Multi-task learning with shared encoder**:
- Single LSTM encodes temporal patterns of snow/weather
- Three separate prediction heads for different tasks
- Joint training with weighted losses
- All three applications benefit from shared representations

---

## 5. Success Metrics (Quantitative)

### Spatial Prediction (Head A)
**Metric**: RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) on test set  
**Target**: RMSE < 20 cm  
**Interpretation**: On average, predictions within ±20 cm of actual snow depth

**Secondary Metrics**:
- MAE (Mean Absolute Error): < 15 cm
- R² (coefficient of determination): > 0.75
- By-region analysis: RMSE < 25 cm in all regions

### Temporal Forecasting (Head B)
**Metric**: RMSE for 7-day ahead forecast  
**Target**: RMSE < 15 cm  
**Interpretation**: At 7-day lead time, predictions within ±15 cm

**Secondary Metrics**:
- Forecast skill score > 0.50 (compared to climatology)
- By-season: Winter RMSE < 12 cm, Spring RMSE < 18 cm
- By-lead-time: 1-day RMSE < 8 cm, 7-day RMSE < 20 cm

### Anomaly Detection (Head D)
**Metrics**: 
- Recall (True Positive Rate): > 70% (catch most events)
- Precision (False Positive Rate): > 70% (avoid false alarms)
- F1 score: > 0.70
- ROC-AUC: > 0.85

**Interpretation**: Detect 70%+ of extreme events without excessive false alarms

### Multi-Task Learning Benefit
**Metric**: Relative improvement  
**Target**: Multi-task model outperforms single-task on all three tasks
- Spatial: +2-5% improvement in R²
- Temporal: +5-10% improvement in RMSE
- Anomaly: +5-10% improvement in F1 score

---

## 6. Assumptions & Constraints

### Assumptions
1. SMHI station snow depth data is reasonably accurate (quality controlled by SMHI)
2. MESAN gridded analysis at 2.5 km resolution faithfully represents local meteorological conditions at station locations (nearest grid cell assumption)
3. Physical relationships between weather/snow are learnable from historical data
4. Historical patterns will generalize to future conditions (limited climate change shift)
5. Geographic features (elevation, latitude) sufficiently capture spatial variability
6. 10 winters (2015-2024) of data is sufficient for robust model training

### Constraints
1. **Spatial Matching**: Nearest MESAN grid cell may not represent station microclimate (2.5 km resolution)
2. **Missing Snow Data**: Station observations have gaps (~5-20% per station); mitigated by coverage filtering and gap interpolation
3. **Geographic Bias**: More stations in populated areas, fewer in mountainous regions
4. **Computational**: Limited GPU budget
5. **Climate Non-Stationarity**: Climate change means old patterns may not fully apply to future winters
6. **Class Imbalance**: Extreme snow events are rare (~3-5% of samples), making anomaly detection challenging

### Mitigations
1. MESAN provides spatially complete meteorological coverage at all 424 stations (vs. ~20% with station data alone)
2. Quality filtering (≥70% winter coverage) and gap interpolation (≤3 days) preserve data integrity
3. Test on geographically diverse stations across full latitude/elevation range
4. Use efficient architectures (LSTM, not transformer) for moderate computational cost
5. Use recent years (2015-2024) to capture current climate patterns
6. Class weighting (pos_weight) and loss rebalancing address anomaly class imbalance

---

## 7. Comparison to Existing Approaches

### Current SMHI Approach
- Operational models based on hydrology + weather rules
- Manual interpolation between stations
- Statistical forecasts (simple linear regression or climatology)

**Limitations**: Limited to simple relationships, labor-intensive, not adaptable

### Academic Baselines
- Distributed hydrological models (complex, many parameters)
- Simple neural networks for snow (single-task, limited data)
- Physics-based models (accurate but computationally expensive)

**Limitations**: Don't use multi-task learning, require many inputs, not optimized for this data

### Our Approach
- Multi-task deep learning (novel combination for snow monitoring)
- Hybrid data: MESAN gridded analysis (features) + SMHI station observations (ground truth)
- Unified architecture for three related tasks (shared LSTM encoder + 3 heads)
- 12 physically meaningful input features from MESAN extraction

**Advantages**: Novel multi-task formulation, rich feature set from MESAN, operationally viable, interpretable via attention weights

---

## 8. Project Scope & Boundaries

### In Scope
- MESAN gridded analysis + SMHI station snow depth data (2015-2024)
- Data pipeline: MESAN extraction, spatial matching, feature engineering
- Multi-task deep learning model development (shared encoder + 3 heads)
- Spatial prediction, temporal forecasting, anomaly detection
- Model evaluation and comparison (multi-task vs. single-task baselines)
- Manuscript preparation and code release

### Out of Scope
- Multiple-year climate projections
- Avalanche mechanics or detailed runout modeling
- Real-time operational deployment (production-ready system)
- Direct satellite imagery (Sentinel-2/SAR) integration
- Global application (Swedish/Nordic region only)  

---

## 9. Expected Outcomes & Impact

### Scientific Impact
- Demonstrates multi-task learning for environmental prediction
- Advances snow hydrology with deep learning
- Published in Q1 journal (IF > 5.0)
- ~20-50 citations over 5 years (typical for applied ML paper)

### Practical Impact
- Operational tool for SMHI water management
- Improved flood/avalanche warning capability
- Open-source code for community use
- ~10-20 adopters (other research groups, agencies)

### Career Impact
- Career progression (solid publication)
- Collaboration with leading ML group (RIDR)
- Visibility in Nordic climate/water research
- Foundation for future PhD/postdoc work

---

## 10. References & Related Work

### Key Papers on Multi-Task Learning
- [Original multi-task learning paper]
- [Ruder et al., overview of multi-task learning]
- [Papers on environmental applications]

### Key Papers on Snow Modeling
- [SMHI hydrology papers]
- [Deep learning for snow]

See PAPER.md for full reference list to build as project progresses.

---

    81→3. LSTM outputs serve as attention **keys** and **values** (shape `(batch, 30, 128)`)
    82→4. Attention produces a weighted summary `attn_out (batch, 128)` — the model learns which of the 30 timesteps are most informative

    85→**Rationale**:
    86→- **LSTM over Transformer**: With 30-step sequences and 12 features, the dataset is not large enough to benefit from full transformer architectures. LSTM provides strong inductive bias for sequential data with fewer parameters.
    87→- **Attention on top of LSTM**: Allows the model to attend to specific days within the 30-day window (e.g., snowfall events, temperature transitions) rather than relying solely on the LSTM's compressed final state.
    88→- **Residual connection**: Preserves the LSTM's sequential summary alongside the attention-based selective summary, preventing information loss.

2. Final hidden state serves as attention **query** (shape `(batch, 1, 128)`)
3. LSTM outputs serve as attention **keys** and **values** (shape `(batch, 30, 128)`)
4. Attention produces a weighted summary `attn_out (batch, 128)` — the model learns which of the 30 timesteps are most informative
5. Residual connection: `attn_out + h_n` → LayerNorm → Dropout → `context`

**Rationale**:
- **LSTM over Transformer**: With 30-step sequences and 12 features, the dataset is not large enough to benefit from full transformer architectures. LSTM provides strong inductive bias for sequential data with fewer parameters.
- **Attention on top of LSTM**: Allows the model to attend to specific days within the 30-day window (e.g., snowfall events, temperature transitions) rather than relying solely on the LSTM's compressed final state.
- **Residual connection**: Preserves the LSTM's sequential summary alongside the attention-based selective summary, preventing information loss.
- **8 attention heads**: Allows different heads to specialize in different temporal patterns (e.g., recent weather vs. accumulated precipitation vs. temperature trends).

### 2.2 Head A: Spatial Prediction (Current Snow Depth)

**Purpose**: Predict current snow depth given 30 days of weather and snow history at a station.

**Architecture** (implemented in `src/models/heads.py :: SpatialHead`):

```
context (128) → Linear(128, 64) → ReLU → Dropout(0.3)
             → Linear(64, 32)   → ReLU → Dropout(0.3)
             → Linear(32, 1)
```

**Input**: Encoder context vector `(batch, 128)`
**Output**: Predicted snow depth `(batch, 1)` — unbounded linear output (cm)
**Target**: Snow depth at day 30 of the input sequence (`target_A`)
**Loss**: MSE

**Rationale**:
- 3-layer MLP with decreasing width (128→64→32→1) provides sufficient capacity for regression while preventing overfitting.
- No output activation — snow depth is non-negative in reality, but the scaler normalizes targets, so the output space is unbounded during training. Predictions are de-normalized for evaluation.
- Dropout at each layer prevents co-adaptation of hidden units.

**Performance**: V7b achieves RMSE **1.01 cm** (R²=0.999) — essentially perfect spatial prediction. This is partly because the input sequence includes `snow_depth_cm` as a feature, providing a strong autoregressive signal (today ≈ yesterday). The spatial task's primary value is forcing the encoder to preserve snow depth information in its representations, which benefits the other heads.

### 2.3 Head B: Temporal Forecasting (7-Day Ahead)

**Purpose**: Forecast snow depth for the next 7 days given 30 days of history.

**Architecture — MLP decoder** (implemented in `src/models/heads.py :: TemporalHeadMLP`):

```
context (128) → Linear(128, 64) → ReLU → Dropout(0.3)
             → Linear(64, 7)
```

**Input**: Encoder context vector `(batch, 128)`
**Output**: 7-day forecast `(batch, 7)` — each value is predicted snow depth (cm)
**Target**: Snow depth at days 31-37 (`target_B`)
**Loss**: MSE (uniform weight across all 7 forecast steps)

**Why MLP, not LSTM decoder**: Three temporal head architectures were tested across V1-V7b:

| Architecture | Version | Params | Temporal RMSE | Rationale |
|-------------|---------|--------|---------------|-----------|
| LSTM decoder | V1, V2 | 25K | 7.01 cm (V2) | Recurrence enables position-dependent outputs but is prone to overfitting |
| **MLP** | **V3, V7, V7b** | **8.8K** | **5.61 cm (V7b)** | **Simpler architecture, 65% fewer params, 20% better RMSE** |
| Autoregressive GRU | V4 | 17K | — (interrupted) | Error accumulates across forecast steps; no benefit observed |

**Why MLP won**:
1. **Less overfitting**: The LSTM decoder's 25K parameters easily memorize temporal patterns. The MLP's 8.8K parameters constrain capacity, forcing the encoder to learn more generalizable representations. Val temporal divergence: LSTM 34→50 (+47%), MLP 33→37 (+12%).
2. **No error accumulation**: The autoregressive decoder feeds predictions back as input, accumulating errors at each step. The MLP predicts all 7 days independently from the context vector.
3. **All 7 days benefit**: V7b MLP beats the LSTM on every forecast day — Day1 (2.78 vs 2.84), Day4 (5.61 vs 6.32), Day7 (7.44 vs 9.25). The improvement grows with horizon because the LSTM decoder overfits more at longer ranges.

**Alternative architectures** (kept in codebase for reference):
- `TemporalHead`: LSTM decoder that repeats context 7 times as input. Provides position-dependent outputs via recurrence but overfits.
- `TemporalHeadAutoregressive`: GRU cell with prediction feedback. Clamps outputs to non-negative (physical constraint). Suffers from error accumulation.

**Purpose**: Detect whether an extreme snow event occurs at the day after the input window.

**Architecture** (implemented in `src/models/heads.py :: AnomalyHead`):

```
context (128) → Linear(128, 64) → ReLU → Dropout(0.3)
             → Linear(64, 32)   → ReLU → Dropout(0.3)
             → Linear(32, 1)    [raw logits]
```

- Despite the AUC ceiling, the anomaly head provides a useful auxiliary training signal that regularizes the shared encoder.

## 3. Data Pipeline

### 3.1 Data Sources

The training pipeline uses two complementary data sources:

| Source | Role | Resolution | Period |
|--------|------|------------|--------|
| **MESAN** (Meteorological Analysis) | Input features | 2.5 km grid, hourly | 2015-2024 |
| **SMHI station observations** | Ground truth targets | Point measurements | 2015-2024 |

**Why this hybrid approach (not station-only or gridded-only)**:

SMHI station data is sparse — only ~20% of Sweden's 1,896 snow stations also measure the meteorological variables needed for ML training (temperature, humidity, wind, etc.). MESAN is a gridded analysis product that combines station data, radar, satellite, and NWP models into a spatially complete, quality-controlled analysis at 2.5 km resolution. By extracting MESAN values at station locations, we get:
- **100% feature coverage** at every station (no NaN for any meteorological variable)
- **424 stations** with snow depth observations (vs. ~10 stations with full meteorological data from station observations alone)
- **Physically consistent** features — MESAN enforces conservation laws and cross-variable consistency

Station snow depth measurements serve as ground truth because MESAN does not directly measure snow depth — it provides only frozen precipitation accumulations, which require a snowpack model to convert to depth.

```
MESAN GRIB (2.5 km, ~30 variables)
       ↓ extract nearest grid cell at each station (lat, lon)
Daily feature vectors (20 columns × 1,896 stations × 2,035 days)
       ↓ left-join on (station_id, date)
Station snow depth observations (659 stations, 1.6M measurements)
       ↓ filter ≥50% winter coverage, interpolate ≤5-day gaps
Training data: 783,879 rows × 21 columns × 424 stations
       ↓ per-station 30-day sequences
Input: (N, 30, 12)  Targets: A(N,), B(N,7), D(N,)
```

### 2.4 Head D: Anomaly Detection (Extreme Snow Events)

**Purpose**: Classify the severity of snow warning events at the day after the input window,
using SMHI Class I/II/III physical criteria as ground truth labels.

**Architecture** (implemented in `src/models/heads.py :: AnomalyHead`):

```
context (64) → Linear(64, 64) → ReLU → Dropout(0.3)
            → Linear(64, 32)  → ReLU → Dropout(0.3)
            → Linear(32, 3)   [raw logits for 3 classes]
```

**Input**: Encoder context vector `(batch, 64)` (V8/V9 with encoder_hidden=64)
**Output**: Class logits `(batch, 3)` — apply softmax for class probabilities
**Target**: Integer label 0/1/2 (`target_D`): 0=Normal, 1=Serious, 2=Extreme
**Loss**: `CrossEntropyLoss` with class weights `[1.0, 12.0, 22.0]` (V9)

#### 2.4.1 Anomaly Label Grounding (V9)

Prior versions (V1–V8) used binary labels (anomaly/normal) with a single threshold
(`snow_change > 20 cm/day`), which missed the majority of SMHI-issued warnings.
V9 introduces 3-class labels grounded in the SMHI Class I/II/III warning criteria:

| Label | Severity | SMHI Basis | Key Rules |
|-------|----------|-----------|-----------|
| 0 | Normal | No warning | Background conditions |
| 1 | Serious | Class I | 5–10 cm/day OR 3-day persistent Class I |
| 2 | Extreme | Class II/III | >10 cm/day, wind-snow (>8 m/s), rapid melt, rain-on-snow |

**Source**: Table 1 of Yang et al. (2023), SMHI Hydrology No. 23.
**Full documentation**: `Docs/ANOMALY_CRITERIA.md`

The wind-snow compound rule (`snow_change > 5 cm/day AND wind_speed > 8 m/s`) uses the
exact SMHI threshold of 8 m/s — directly from the official warning criteria.

#### 2.4.2 SMHI System Change (Oct 26, 2021)

SMHI transitioned to an impact-based Yellow/Orange/Red system on Oct 26, 2021. Our model
covers 2015–2024, crossing this boundary. We apply the pre-2021 Class I/II/III physical
thresholds throughout because:
- They are publicly documented and reproducible
- The post-2021 thresholds are regionally adapted and not public
- **Class I ≠ Yellow, Class II ≠ Orange** — there is no direct mapping

#### 2.4.3 Loss Function Evolution

| Version | Loss | Target | AUC/F1 | Issue |
|---------|------|--------|---------|-------|
| V2–V6 | BCE (pos_weight=10) | Binary 0/1 | AUC 0.726–0.765 | Only Class III captured |
| V7b | BCE (pos_weight=25) | Binary 0/1 | AUC 0.770 | Class I/II missed |
| V8 | BCE (pos_weight=25) | Binary 0/1 | AUC 0.803 | Class I/II missed, no severity |
| **V9** | **CrossEntropy [1,12,22]** | **3-class 0/1/2** | **macro-F1 target ≥0.55** | Full SMHI alignment |

Class weights `[1.0, 12.0, 22.0]` are inverse-frequency estimates for ~89/7/4% distribution.
These are initial values to be refined after observing actual label counts from V9 data.

**Why CrossEntropyLoss works where Focal failed**: Focal loss (V3/V4) failed because it
reduced each sample's loss contribution — bringing the anomaly loss magnitude to ~0.018,
compared to ~35 for MSE_B. This made the anomaly gradient negligible. CrossEntropyLoss
maintains loss magnitudes comparable to BCE (~1.0), keeping the anomaly contribution
visible in the multi-task gradient balance.

**Anomaly as a forecasting task**: The label `target_D` is computed at day 31 — the day
after the 30-day input window. The model must **predict** future extreme events from
current conditions. This limits achievable performance; a binary AUC ceiling of ~0.80–0.85
is estimated. For 3-class macro-F1, the target of ≥0.55 accounts for the harder Serious
class (which requires distinguishing from both Normal and Extreme).

- The head catches ~62% of extreme events with AUC=0.770, which has practical value for early warning systems.
- Removing the anomaly head was never tested because it provides training signal diversity without harming the regression tasks.

### 2.4 Head D: Anomaly Detection (Extreme Snow Events)

**Purpose**: Classify the severity of snow warning events at the day after the input window,
using SMHI Class I/II/III physical criteria as ground truth labels.

**Architecture** (implemented in `src/models/heads.py :: AnomalyHead`):

```
context (64) → Linear(64, 64) → ReLU → Dropout(0.3)
            → Linear(64, 32)  → ReLU → Dropout(0.3)
            → Linear(32, 3)   [raw logits for 3 classes]
```

**Input**: Encoder context vector `(batch, 64)` (V8/V9 with encoder_hidden=64)
**Output**: Class logits `(batch, 3)` — apply softmax for class probabilities
**Target**: Integer label 0/1/2 (`target_D`): 0=Normal, 1=Serious, 2=Extreme
**Loss**: `CrossEntropyLoss` with class weights `[1.0, 12.0, 22.0]` (V9)

#### 2.4.1 Anomaly Label Grounding (V9)

Prior versions (V1–V8) used binary labels (anomaly/normal) with a single threshold
(`snow_change > 20 cm/day`), which missed the majority of SMHI-issued warnings.
V9 introduces 3-class labels grounded in the SMHI Class I/II/III warning criteria:

| Label | Severity | SMHI Basis | Key Rules |
|-------|----------|-----------|-----------|
| 0 | Normal | No warning | Background conditions |
| 1 | Serious | Class I | 5–10 cm/day OR 3-day persistent Class I |
| 2 | Extreme | Class II/III | >10 cm/day, wind-snow (>8 m/s), rapid melt, rain-on-snow |

**Source**: Table 1 of Yang et al. (2023), SMHI Hydrology No. 23.
**Full documentation**: `Docs/ANOMALY_CRITERIA.md`

The wind-snow compound rule (`snow_change > 5 cm/day AND wind_speed > 8 m/s`) uses the
exact SMHI threshold of 8 m/s — directly from the official warning criteria.

#### 2.4.2 SMHI System Change (Oct 26, 2021)

SMHI transitioned to an impact-based Yellow/Orange/Red system on Oct 26, 2021. Our model
covers 2015–2024, crossing this boundary. We apply the pre-2021 Class I/II/III physical
thresholds throughout because:
- They are publicly documented and reproducible
- The post-2021 thresholds are regionally adapted and not public
- **Class I ≠ Yellow, Class II ≠ Orange** — there is no direct mapping

#### 2.4.3 Loss Function Evolution

| Version | Loss | Target | AUC/F1 | Issue |
|---------|------|--------|---------|-------|
| V2–V6 | BCE (pos_weight=10) | Binary 0/1 | AUC 0.726–0.765 | Only Class III captured |
| V7b | BCE (pos_weight=25) | Binary 0/1 | AUC 0.770 | Class I/II missed |
| V8 | BCE (pos_weight=25) | Binary 0/1 | AUC 0.803 | Class I/II missed, no severity |
| **V9** | **CrossEntropy [1,12,22]** | **3-class 0/1/2** | **macro-F1 target ≥0.55** | Full SMHI alignment |

Class weights `[1.0, 12.0, 22.0]` are inverse-frequency estimates for ~89/7/4% distribution.
These are initial values to be refined after observing actual label counts from V9 data.

**Why CrossEntropyLoss works where Focal failed**: Focal loss (V3/V4) failed because it
reduced each sample's loss contribution — bringing the anomaly loss magnitude to ~0.018,
compared to ~35 for MSE_B. This made the anomaly gradient negligible. CrossEntropyLoss
maintains loss magnitudes comparable to BCE (~1.0), keeping the anomaly contribution
visible in the multi-task gradient balance.

**Anomaly as a forecasting task**: The label `target_D` is computed at day 31 — the day
after the 30-day input window. The model must **predict** future extreme events from
current conditions. This limits achievable performance; a binary AUC ceiling of ~0.80–0.85
is estimated. For 3-class macro-F1, the target of ≥0.55 accounts for the harder Serious
class (which requires distinguishing from both Normal and Extreme).

# Technical Methodology

## 1. Architecture Overview

### 1.1 High-Level Design

```
              MESAN Gridded Analysis (2.5 km, hourly)
           extracted at SMHI snow station locations
                          ↓
      Station snow depth observations (ground truth)
                          ↓
              ┌─────────────────────┐
              │  DATA PREPROCESSING  │
              │ - Per-station seqs   │
              │ - StandardScaler     │
              │ - Continuity check   │
              └──────────┬──────────┘
                         ↓
            (batch, 30 days, 12 features)
                         ↓
              ┌──────────────────────┐
              │   SHARED ENCODER     │
              │  LSTM (2-layer, 128) │
              │  + MultiheadAttn (8) │
              │  + LayerNorm         │
              │  + Residual + Drop   │
              └──────────┬───────────┘
                         ↓
              context (batch, 128)
                         ↓
       ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
       ↓                 ↓                 ↓
    HEAD A           HEAD B             HEAD D
   (Spatial)       (Temporal)          (Anomaly)
   3-layer MLP     2-layer MLP         3-layer MLP
   128→64→32→1     128→64→7            128→64→32→1
       ↓                 ↓                 ↓
   Snow depth at   Snow depth 1-7     Extreme event
   current time    days ahead          logits
    (b, 1)          (b, 7)             (b, 1)
```

### 1.2 Rationale for Multi-Task Learning

The three tasks are interconnected through shared snow physics:

- **Spatial prediction** requires understanding how current weather conditions relate to snow accumulation and melt — the same thermodynamic relationships govern future snow evolution.
- **Temporal forecasting** benefits from spatial context — a model that understands snow depth patterns across conditions can better extrapolate forward in time.
- **Anomaly detection** identifies unusual deviations from the patterns learned by the spatial and temporal tasks. Shared representations allow the anomaly head to leverage learned "normal" behavior.

The shared encoder forces the model to learn generalizable snow physics representations rather than task-specific shortcuts. This is particularly valuable given the limited amount of extreme event data (anomalies are ~3.6% of samples), where the encoder benefits from the abundant regression signal.

**Empirical validation**: Over 8 versions (V1-V7b), gradient balance between tasks proved critical. When one task dominated the shared encoder's gradients, all tasks suffered. The final V7b configuration achieves the best results on all three tasks simultaneously, confirming that proper gradient balance enables positive transfer.

---

## 2. Model Components

### 2.1 Shared Encoder

**Purpose**: Learn temporal patterns and snow physics representations from daily weather time series.

**Architecture** (implemented in `src/models/encoder.py`):

| Component | Details |
|-----------|---------|
| LSTM | 2 layers, hidden size 128, batch-first, inter-layer dropout 0.3 |
| Cross-Attention | `nn.MultiheadAttention` with 8 heads; query=final hidden state, key/value=LSTM outputs |
| Normalization | `nn.LayerNorm` on attention output |
| Residual connection | Attention output added to LSTM final hidden state before LayerNorm |
| Dropout | Applied after LayerNorm, before output (p=0.3) |
| Bidirectional | Optional (default off); when on, linear projection maps `2×hidden` → `hidden` |

**Input**: `(batch_size, seq_len=30, n_features=12)`
**Output**: `context` vector of shape `(batch_size, 128)`

**Forward pass logic**:
1. LSTM processes full input sequence → `lstm_out (batch, 30, 128)`, final hidden state `h_n`
2. Final hidden state serves as attention **query** (shape `(batch, 1, 128)`)
3. LSTM outputs serve as attention **keys** and **values** (shape `(batch, 30, 128)`)
4. Attention produces a weighted summary `attn_out (batch, 128)` — the model learns which of the 30 timesteps are most informative
5. Residual connection: `attn_out + h_n` → LayerNorm → Dropout → `context`

**Rationale**:
- **LSTM over Transformer**: With 30-step sequences and 12 features, the dataset is not large enough to benefit from full transformer architectures. LSTM provides strong inductive bias for sequential data with fewer parameters.
- **Attention on top of LSTM**: Allows the model to attend to specific days within the 30-day window (e.g., snowfall events, temperature transitions) rather than relying solely on the LSTM's compressed final state.
- **Residual connection**: Preserves the LSTM's sequential summary alongside the attention-based selective summary, preventing information loss.
- **8 attention heads**: Allows different heads to specialize in different temporal patterns (e.g., recent weather vs. accumulated precipitation vs. temperature trends).

### 2.2 Head A: Spatial Prediction (Current Snow Depth)

**Purpose**: Predict current snow depth given 30 days of weather and snow history at a station.

**Architecture** (implemented in `src/models/heads.py :: SpatialHead`):

```
context (128) → Linear(128, 64) → ReLU → Dropout(0.3)
             → Linear(64, 32)   → ReLU → Dropout(0.3)
             → Linear(32, 1)
```

**Input**: Encoder context vector `(batch, 128)`
**Output**: Predicted snow depth `(batch, 1)` — unbounded linear output (cm)
**Target**: Snow depth at day 30 of the input sequence (`target_A`)
**Loss**: MSE

**Rationale**:
- 3-layer MLP with decreasing width (128→64→32→1) provides sufficient capacity for regression while preventing overfitting.
- No output activation — snow depth is non-negative in reality, but the scaler normalizes targets, so the output space is unbounded during training. Predictions are de-normalized for evaluation.
- Dropout at each layer prevents co-adaptation of hidden units.

**Performance**: V7b achieves RMSE **1.01 cm** (R²=0.999) — essentially perfect spatial prediction. This is partly because the input sequence includes `snow_depth_cm` as a feature, providing a strong autoregressive signal (today ≈ yesterday). The spatial task's primary value is forcing the encoder to preserve snow depth information in its representations, which benefits the other heads.

### 2.3 Head B: Temporal Forecasting (7-Day Ahead)

**Purpose**: Forecast snow depth for the next 7 days given 30 days of history.

**Architecture — MLP decoder** (implemented in `src/models/heads.py :: TemporalHeadMLP`):

```
context (128) → Linear(128, 64) → ReLU → Dropout(0.3)
             → Linear(64, 7)
```

**Input**: Encoder context vector `(batch, 128)`
**Output**: 7-day forecast `(batch, 7)` — each value is predicted snow depth (cm)
**Target**: Snow depth at days 31-37 (`target_B`)
**Loss**: MSE (uniform weight across all 7 forecast steps)

**Why MLP, not LSTM decoder**: Three temporal head architectures were tested across V1-V7b:

| Architecture | Version | Params | Temporal RMSE | Rationale |
|-------------|---------|--------|---------------|-----------|
| LSTM decoder | V1, V2 | 25K | 7.01 cm (V2) | Recurrence enables position-dependent outputs but is prone to overfitting |
| **MLP** | **V3, V7, V7b** | **8.8K** | **5.61 cm (V7b)** | **Simpler architecture, 65% fewer params, 20% better RMSE** |
| Autoregressive GRU | V4 | 17K | — (interrupted) | Error accumulates across forecast steps; no benefit observed |

**Why MLP won**:
1. **Less overfitting**: The LSTM decoder's 25K parameters easily memorize temporal patterns. The MLP's 8.8K parameters constrain capacity, forcing the encoder to learn more generalizable representations. Val temporal divergence: LSTM 34→50 (+47%), MLP 33→37 (+12%).
2. **No error accumulation**: The autoregressive decoder feeds predictions back as input, accumulating errors at each step. The MLP predicts all 7 days independently from the context vector.
3. **All 7 days benefit**: V7b MLP beats the LSTM on every forecast day — Day1 (2.78 vs 2.84), Day4 (5.61 vs 6.32), Day7 (7.44 vs 9.25). The improvement grows with horizon because the LSTM decoder overfits more at longer ranges.

**Alternative architectures** (kept in codebase for reference):
- `TemporalHead`: LSTM decoder that repeats context 7 times as input. Provides position-dependent outputs via recurrence but overfits.
- `TemporalHeadAutoregressive`: GRU cell with prediction feedback. Clamps outputs to non-negative (physical constraint). Suffers from error accumulation.

### 2.4 Head D: Anomaly Detection (Extreme Snow Events)

**Purpose**: Detect whether an extreme snow event occurs at the day after the input window.

**Architecture** (implemented in `src/models/heads.py :: AnomalyHead`):

```
context (128) → Linear(128, 64) → ReLU → Dropout(0.3)
             → Linear(64, 32)   → ReLU → Dropout(0.3)
             → Linear(32, 1)    [raw logits]
```

**Input**: Encoder context vector `(batch, 128)`
**Output**: Raw logits `(batch, 1)` — apply sigmoid for probability
**Target**: Binary label 0/1 (`target_D`)
**Loss**: `BCEWithLogitsLoss` with `pos_weight=25.0`

**Why BCE, not Focal loss**: Two anomaly loss functions were tested:

| Loss | Version | Anomaly F1 | AUC | Raw Loss Magnitude | Problem |
|------|---------|-----------|-----|-------------------|---------|
| **BCE** (pos_weight=25) | **V2, V7, V7b** | **0.220** | **0.770** | 0.8-1.0 | None — works well |
| Focal (α=0.75, γ=2) | V3, V4 | 0.076 | 0.726 | **0.018** | Loss magnitude 50x too small for multi-task training |

**Why focal loss failed**: Focal loss reduces the contribution of easy-to-classify examples, but in a multi-task setting this is catastrophic. With MSE_B ≈ 35-40, focal loss at 0.018 contributes only 0.04 to the total gradient even with λ_D=2.0 — that's 0.3% of the gradient, effectively invisible to the optimizer. BCE at ~1.0 contributes 2.0 (14% of gradient), which is sufficient for learning.

**Why pos_weight=25**: The anomaly class rate is 3.6% (96.4% negative). The inverse class ratio is 96.4/3.6 ≈ 27. Using `pos_weight=25` makes each positive sample count 25× in the loss, approximately balancing the class contributions. V7b achieves recall=0.619 (62% of anomalies detected) with this setting.

**Anomaly as a forecasting task**: The anomaly label `target_D` is computed at day 31 (the day after the 30-day input window), not within the window. This means the model must **predict** future extreme events from current conditions, not merely **detect** them. This explains the AUC ceiling at ~0.77 — some extreme events are genuinely unpredictable from 30-day weather history alone.

**Rationale for keeping the anomaly head**:
- Despite the AUC ceiling, the anomaly head provides a useful auxiliary training signal that regularizes the shared encoder.
- The head catches ~62% of extreme events with AUC=0.770, which has practical value for early warning systems.
- Removing the anomaly head was never tested because it provides training signal diversity without harming the regression tasks.

---

## 3. Data Pipeline

### 3.1 Data Sources

The training pipeline uses two complementary data sources:

| Source | Role | Resolution | Period |
|--------|------|------------|--------|
| **MESAN** (Meteorological Analysis) | Input features | 2.5 km grid, hourly | 2015-2024 |
| **SMHI station observations** | Ground truth targets | Point measurements | 2015-2024 |

**Why this hybrid approach (not station-only or gridded-only)**:

SMHI station data is sparse — only ~20% of Sweden's 1,896 snow stations also measure the meteorological variables needed for ML training (temperature, humidity, wind, etc.). MESAN is a gridded analysis product that combines station data, radar, satellite, and NWP models into a spatially complete, quality-controlled analysis at 2.5 km resolution. By extracting MESAN values at station locations, we get:
- **100% feature coverage** at every station (no NaN for any meteorological variable)
- **424 stations** with snow depth observations (vs. ~10 stations with full meteorological data from station observations alone)
- **Physically consistent** features — MESAN enforces conservation laws and cross-variable consistency

Station snow depth measurements serve as ground truth because MESAN does not directly measure snow depth — it provides only frozen precipitation accumulations, which require a snowpack model to convert to depth.

```
MESAN GRIB (2.5 km, ~30 variables)
       ↓ extract nearest grid cell at each station (lat, lon)
Daily feature vectors (20 columns × 1,896 stations × 2,035 days)
       ↓ left-join on (station_id, date)
Station snow depth observations (659 stations, 1.6M measurements)
       ↓ filter ≥50% winter coverage, interpolate ≤5-day gaps
Training data: 783,879 rows × 21 columns × 424 stations
       ↓ per-station 30-day sequences
Input: (N, 30, 12)  Targets: A(N,), B(N,7), D(N,)
```

### 3.2 Input Features (12 total)

The model uses 12 features selected for physical relevance to snow processes:

| # | Feature | Source | Unit | Physical Rationale |
|---|---------|--------|------|-------------------|
| 1 | `snow_depth_cm` | Station obs | cm | Primary target; autoregressive input — recent snow depth is the strongest predictor of near-future depth |
| 2 | `temperature` | MESAN `t` (2m) | C | Governs melt/freeze threshold; converted from Kelvin |
| 3 | `precipitation` | MESAN `prec24h` | mm | 24h accumulated; drives snow accumulation (when cold) or melt acceleration (when warm) |
| 4 | `wind_speed` | MESAN `u`,`v` (10m) | m/s | Computed as sqrt(u^2+v^2); wind redistribution and sublimation affect snow depth |
| 5 | `humidity` | MESAN `r` (2m) | % | High humidity slows sublimation; low humidity accelerates it. Converted from fraction ×100 |
| 6 | `frozen_precip` | MESAN `frsn24h` | cm | 24h frozen precipitation; direct snowfall indicator, distinguishes snow from rain |
| 7 | `visibility` | MESAN `vis` | km | Proxy for active precipitation and fog/low cloud; converted from m ÷1000, capped at 100 km |
| 8 | `cloud_cover` | MESAN `tcc` | % | Total cloud cover; modulates radiative cooling (clear skies → faster melt) |
| 9 | `day_sin` | Derived | [-1, 1] | sin(2π × day_of_year / 365.25) — cyclical annual position |
| 10 | `day_cos` | Derived | [-1, 1] | cos(2π × day_of_year / 365.25) — together with day_sin, uniquely encodes calendar date |
| 11 | `latitude` | Metadata | deg | Station latitude (55.3-68.9 N); controls solar angle, daylight hours, climate zone |
| 12 | `elevation` | Metadata | m | Station elevation (-1 to 1220 m); strong predictor of temperature and snow line |

**Why 12 features (not the original 9)**: The original design used 9 features based on available station data. MESAN provides 3 additional physically meaningful variables that directly relate to snow processes:
- `frozen_precip` distinguishes snowfall from rainfall — critical for Sweden where precipitation type varies dramatically with latitude and elevation.
- `visibility` serves as a proxy for active precipitation events (low visibility = active snowfall/rain).
- `cloud_cover` modulates radiative balance — clear skies in winter can mean rapid cooling (preserving snow) or strong solar radiation in spring (accelerating melt).

**Features considered but excluded**: `wind_gust`, `temp_min`, `temp_max`, `ground_temp`, `precip_type`, `precip_sort`, `longitude` — available in the MESAN extraction (20 columns total) but excluded to avoid redundancy and keep the feature space manageable.

### 3.3 Preprocessing

**Normalization** (implemented in `src/data/preprocessors.py :: SnowDataPreprocessor`):

```
feature_normalized = (feature - mean_train) / std_train
```

- StandardScaler is fitted **only on training data** to prevent information leakage from validation/test sets.
- The fitted scaler (mean and scale arrays) is saved to disk alongside the trained model for inference-time use.

**Why StandardScaler (not MinMaxScaler or RobustScaler)**: StandardScaler centers features at zero with unit variance, which is optimal for LSTM + attention architectures where the tanh/sigmoid activations operate best near zero. Snow depth has extreme outliers (max 229 cm vs mean 13 cm), but StandardScaler handles these adequately for the LSTM's gradient flow.

**Missing value handling** (applied per-feature):

1. Linear interpolation for gaps ≤ 5 days (preserves trends)
2. Forward fill (`ffill`) for remaining isolated gaps
3. Backward fill (`bfill`) for gaps at the start of a station's record
4. Fill remaining NaN with 0 (rare; only if entire feature is missing)

**Why interpolation ≤ 5 days**: MESAN gridded data has 100% coverage — it never has NaN for meteorological variables. Missing values only occur in the snow depth column (station observations). Gaps of 5 days or less are interpolated because snow depth changes slowly enough that linear interpolation introduces minimal error. Gaps >5 days are too uncertain and are treated as segment breaks.

### 3.4 Sequence Creation

Sequences are created **per station** to prevent mixing data across stations:

```python
for each station:
    sort by date
    for i in range(len(station_data) - seq_length - forecast_horizon):
        input  = features[i : i + 30]                    # 30-day window
        target_A = snow_depth[i + 29]                     # last day of window
        target_B = snow_depth[i + 30 : i + 37]            # next 7 days
        target_D = anomaly_label[i + 30]                  # next day anomaly
```

**Continuity checking**: Before sequence creation, each station's time series is segmented at gaps > 3 days. Only contiguous segments with ≥38 days (30 seq + 7 forecast + 1 buffer) produce valid sequences. This prevents the model from learning across data gaps.

**Why per-station (not pooled)**: Creating sequences across station boundaries would produce physically meaningless transitions (e.g., jumping from a coastal station at 0m to a mountain station at 1000m). Per-station grouping ensures each sequence represents a coherent physical location. The model generalizes across stations via the shared encoder, not by mixing station data in individual sequences.

### 3.5 Anomaly Labels

Binary labels for extreme snow events are computed from the raw (un-normalized) data using physically motivated thresholds:

| Event Type | Condition | Physical Rationale |
|------------|-----------|-------------------|
| Heavy snowfall | snow increase > 20 cm/day | Extreme accumulation exceeding typical daily rates (~2-5 cm) |
| Heavy frozen precip | `frozen_precip` > 5 cm/24h | Direct MESAN measurement of extreme snowfall |
| Rapid melt | snow decrease > 5 cm/day for 3+ consecutive days | Sustained warm spell causing dangerous melt (flood risk) |
| Rain on snow | temp > 0 AND precip > 5mm AND snow > 10cm | Warm rain on existing snowpack — triggers rapid densification and potential flooding |
| Warm ground melt | `ground_temp` > 2C AND snow decrease > 5 cm/day AND snow > 10cm | Basal melt from warm ground, distinct from surface melt |

**Anomaly as a forecasting task**: The anomaly label `target_D` is computed at position `i+30` — the day **after** the input sequence ends. This means the model must predict future extreme events from the 30-day weather history, not detect current events. This design choice has significant implications:
- The task is inherently harder than detection (some events are genuinely unpredictable).
- ROC-AUC is empirically capped at ~0.77 across all training versions (V1-V7b), confirmed by consistent results regardless of loss function, weight, or architecture changes.
- This ceiling is a **task limitation**, not a model limitation — the input signal simply doesn't contain sufficient information to predict all future extreme events.

**Why these thresholds**: Calibrated for Swedish conditions where typical winter snowfall is 2-5 cm/day and melt rates of 5+ cm/day indicate significant events. Expected anomaly rate: ~3.6% of samples (sufficient for learning but genuinely rare events).

### 3.6 Data Splits

**Strategy**: Temporal split by year to prevent data leakage.

| Split | Years | Samples | Rationale |
|-------|-------|---------|-----------|
| **Training** | 2015-2022 (8 winters) | 635,813 | Largest portion for learning; includes diverse snow conditions |
| **Validation** | 2023 (1 winter) | 64,940 | Hyperparameter tuning and early stopping; recent year for realistic evaluation |
| **Test** | 2024 (1 winter) | 31,822 | Final held-out evaluation; never used during training or tuning |

**Why temporal (not random) splitting**:
- Random splitting would leak future information into training — the model could learn patterns from nearby dates in validation/test sets.
- Temporal splitting simulates the real deployment scenario: the model is trained on historical data and must predict a future winter it has never seen.
- All stations appear in all splits (station-stratified), so the model sees each station's training history but must generalize to unseen time periods.

---

## 4. Training Procedure

### 4.1 Loss Functions

#### Head A Loss (Spatial)
```
L_A = MSE(pred_A, target_A) = mean((pred - true)^2)
```
Standard MSE penalizes large errors quadratically, appropriate for snow depth where large errors matter more than small ones.

#### Head B Loss (Temporal)
```
L_B = MSE(pred_B, target_B) = mean over batch and 7 timesteps of (pred - true)^2
```
Uniform weight across all 7 forecast steps. An optional weighted variant (`TemporalLoss` in `src/models/losses.py`) can weight later predictions more heavily, but the default treats all horizons equally.

**Why uniform weighting**: Equal weights across all 7 days performed best empirically. The MLP head naturally produces increasing error with horizon (Day1=2.78 cm → Day7=7.44 cm), and the uniform loss allows the model to allocate capacity freely across horizons. Weighting later days more heavily was not tested because the MLP head already shows healthy skill decay (1.68 ratio, not excessive).

#### Head D Loss (Anomaly)
```
L_D = BCEWithLogitsLoss(pred_D, target_D, pos_weight=25)
     = -25 * y * log(σ(z)) - (1-y) * log(1-σ(z))
```
`BCEWithLogitsLoss` combines sigmoid activation with binary cross-entropy in a numerically stable way. The `pos_weight=25` makes each positive (anomaly) sample count 25× in the loss, compensating for the 3.6% anomaly rate (inverse ratio ≈ 27).

#### Combined Multi-Task Loss
```
L_total = λ_A * L_A + λ_B * L_B + λ_D * L_D
```

### 4.2 Loss Weight Evolution (V1→V7b)

Finding the right loss weights was the most critical optimization across all versions. The core challenge: **raw MSE_B is 17-20× larger than MSE_A**, so even small λ_B values give temporal an outsized gradient share.

| Version | λ_A | λ_B | λ_D | Anomaly Loss | Eff. Gradient: A% / B% / D% | Spatial RMSE | Temporal RMSE | Anomaly F1 |
|---------|-----|-----|-----|-------------|------------------------------|-------------|--------------|-----------|
| V1 | 1.0 | 1.0 | 0.3 | BCE pw=10 | 36 / 63 / 0.2 | 1.29 | 7.66 | 0.199 |
| V2 | 1.0 | 0.3 | 2.0 | BCE pw=25 | 5 / 81 / 15 | 1.21 | 7.01 | 0.232 |
| V3 | 1.0 | 0.3 | 2.0 | Focal | 12 / 88 / **0.3** | 1.10 | 6.40 | 0.076 |
| V5 | — | — | — | BCE pw=25 | Uncertainty (drifts) | 1.21 | 7.38 | 0.149 |
| V6 | — | — | — | BCE pw=10 | Uncertainty (drifts) | 1.47 | 6.13 | 0.167 |
| V7 | 1.0 | 0.3 | 2.0 | BCE pw=25 | 14 / 72 / 12 | 1.07 | 6.40 | 0.201 |
| **V7b** | **1.0** | **0.1** | **2.0** | **BCE pw=25** | **27 / 48 / 25** | **1.01** | **5.61** | **0.220** |

**Key findings from this progression**:

1. **Temporal always dominated the gradient** (V1-V7): Even at λ_B=0.3, temporal contributed 72-88% of the gradient because MSE_B ≈ 35 while MSE_A ≈ 2. Only at λ_B=0.1 (V7b) does temporal drop to 48% — still the largest share, but no longer overwhelming.

2. **All tasks benefit from balance** (V7b): Reducing temporal from 72% to 48% improved spatial (-5.6%), temporal (-12.3%), AND anomaly (+2.2% AUC). The encoder learns better representations when not dominated by a single task.

3. **Focal loss is incompatible with multi-task training** (V3-V4): Focal loss reduces easy-example gradients to near-zero. In a multi-task setting where the other tasks produce gradients 50× larger, this makes the focal-loss task invisible. V3 anomaly F1 collapsed from 0.232 to 0.076.

4. **Uncertainty-weighted loss is structurally unsuitable** (V5-V6): Kendall et al.'s uncertainty weighting (L = Σ exp(-s_i)*L_i + s_i) was tested in V5 and V6. It failed because the optimizer drifts log-variance parameters to minimize the total loss, which systematically down-weights high-variance tasks (MSE regression) and up-weights low-variance tasks (BCE classification). V6's spatial weight dropped from 0.37 to 0.05 in 26 epochs, starving the spatial head. Conclusion: uncertainty weighting requires homogeneous loss types across tasks.

### 4.3 Optimization

| Parameter | V1 | V2-V7b (current) | Why changed |
|-----------|-----|-------------------|-------------|
| **Optimizer** | AdamW | AdamW | Decouples weight decay from gradient updates; unchanged |
| **Learning rate** | 1e-3 | 3e-4 | V1's 1e-3 caused rapid memorization (best epoch 1). 3e-4 allows longer useful training |
| **Weight decay** | 1e-5 | 1e-4 | 10× stronger L2 regularization; prevents large weight magnitudes |
| **Batch size** | 64 | 64 | Unchanged; stable gradient estimates with 635K training samples |
| **Max epochs** | 100 | 150 | More epochs for lower LR; early stopping prevents wasted compute |
| **Gradient clipping** | 1.0 | 1.0 | Unchanged; prevents exploding LSTM gradients |

**Why AdamW over Adam**: AdamW decouples weight decay from the adaptive learning rate, providing more consistent regularization. This matters for multi-task training where different parameter groups (encoder, heads, loss params) have different gradient magnitudes.

**Learning rate schedule — ReduceLROnPlateau**:
- Monitor: validation total loss
- Factor: 0.5 (halve LR on plateau)
- Patience: 7 epochs before reducing
- Minimum LR: 1e-6

**Why plateau (not cosine) scheduler**: Both were tested:
- **Plateau (V2, V3, V7, V7b)**: Adapts to actual training dynamics; only reduces LR when progress stalls. Best epoch: 5-8.
- **Cosine (V5, V6)**: Smooth decay over all epochs. With uncertainty weighting, cosine kept LR high early, contributing to weight drift. Best epoch: 1-2.

Plateau won because it lets the model train at full LR until validation loss plateaus, then carefully reduces. With fixed weights and MLP head, this produces the most stable training dynamics (V7b best at epoch 8 — the latest best epoch across all versions).

### 4.4 Regularization

| Technique | V1 | V2+ (current) | Why changed |
|-----------|-----|---------------|-------------|
| **Dropout** | p=0.2 | p=0.3 | Stronger regularization to combat temporal overfitting |
| **Weight decay** | 1e-5 | 1e-4 | 10× stronger L2 penalty reduces memorization |
| **Early stopping** | patience=50 | patience=25 | V1 proved 50 was wasteful (best model at epoch 1); 25 is sufficient |
| **LayerNorm** | Encoder attention | Same | Stabilizes training; placed after residual connection |
| **Gradient clipping** | max_norm=1.0 | Same | Prevents gradient explosions in LSTM backpropagation |

**Why dropout=0.3 (not 0.2 or 0.4)**: V1 with p=0.2 showed severe temporal overfitting (train B dropped 48→16 while val B rose 34→50). Increasing to p=0.3 reduced this divergence. p=0.4 was not tested because temporal overfitting was primarily addressed by the MLP head and λ_B reduction, making further dropout increase unnecessary.

### 4.5 Training Dynamics

The typical V7b training curve:

```
Epoch 1:  Train 6.43 (A:28.3 B:54.1 D:0.95)  Val 5.85 (A:4.0 B:38.3 D:0.94)
Epoch 8:  Train 4.07 (A:22.0 B:18.3 D:0.66)  Val 4.29 (A:1.1 B:33.0 D:0.88) ← BEST
Epoch 33: Train 3.51 (A:21.5 B:14.5 D:0.48)  Val 5.22 (A:3.0 B:37.3 D:1.00) ← Early stop
```

Key observations:
- **Best model at epoch 8**: The latest best epoch across all versions, indicating the most stable training dynamics.
- **Val temporal divergence**: 33→37 (+12%). Compared to V7's 34→44 (+29%) and V1's 34→50 (+47%). MLP head + λ_B=0.1 dramatically reduces temporal overfitting.
- **Train anomaly loss drops steadily**: 0.95→0.48, indicating the model learns anomaly patterns. Val anomaly loss stays stable (~0.88-1.00), indicating the learned patterns partially generalize.

---

## 5. Evaluation Metrics

### 5.1 Regression Metrics (Heads A & B)

| Metric | Formula | Interpretation |
|--------|---------|---------------|
| **RMSE** | sqrt(mean((pred - true)^2)) | Average prediction error in cm; penalizes large errors |
| **MAE** | mean(abs(pred - true)) | Median-like error measure in cm; robust to outliers |
| **R²** | 1 - SS_res / SS_tot | Fraction of variance explained (0 = useless, 1 = perfect) |
| **Bias** | mean(pred - true) | Systematic over/under prediction in cm |

### 5.2 Classification Metrics (Head D)

| Metric | Formula | Interpretation |
|--------|---------|---------------|
| **Precision** | TP / (TP + FP) | Of predicted anomalies, what fraction were real? |
| **Recall** | TP / (TP + FN) | Of real anomalies, what fraction were detected? |
| **F1** | 2 * P * R / (P + R) | Harmonic mean balancing precision and recall |
| **ROC-AUC** | Area under ROC curve | Overall discriminative ability (0.5 = random, 1.0 = perfect) |

### 5.3 Final Performance (V7b — Publication Model)

| Task | Metric | V7b Result | Original Target | Status |
|------|--------|-----------|----------------|--------|
| Head A (Spatial) | RMSE | **1.01 cm** | < 20 cm | Exceeds by 20× |
| Head A (Spatial) | R² | **0.999** | — | Near-perfect |
| Head B (Temporal) | Overall RMSE | **5.61 cm** | < 15 cm | Exceeds by 2.7× |
| Head B (Temporal) | Day 1 RMSE | **2.78 cm** | — | Strong short-range |
| Head B (Temporal) | Day 7 RMSE | **7.44 cm** | — | Reasonable long-range |
| Head D (Anomaly) | Recall | **0.619** | > 70% | Below target (ceiling ~0.77 AUC) |
| Head D (Anomaly) | F1 | **0.220** | > 0.70 | Below target (forecasting limitation) |
| Head D (Anomaly) | ROC-AUC | **0.770** | — | Near ceiling |

**Why anomaly targets were not met**: The original targets (recall > 70%, F1 > 0.70) assumed anomaly detection within the input window. The actual implementation predicts anomalies at day 31 (forecasting), which is fundamentally harder. The AUC ceiling of ~0.77 was confirmed across 8 versions with different architectures, loss functions, and weights. This is a task definition limitation, not a model architecture limitation. For publication, the anomaly task is reframed as "extreme event forecasting" with AUC=0.770 as the primary metric.

---

## 6. Baseline Comparisons

### 6.1 Single-Task Baselines

Each baseline uses the **identical encoder architecture** but is trained on only one task:

| Baseline | Architecture | Training |
|----------|-------------|----------|
| Spatial only | SharedEncoder → SpatialHead | MSE on target_A only |
| Temporal only | SharedEncoder → TemporalHeadMLP | MSE on target_B only |
| Anomaly only | SharedEncoder → AnomalyHead | BCE on target_D only |

**Why same architecture**: Using the same architecture isolates the effect of multi-task learning. If the multi-task model outperforms single-task baselines, the improvement comes from shared representations, not architectural differences.

The `SingleTaskModel` class in `src/models/multitask.py` and `SingleTaskTrainer` in `src/training/trainer.py` implement these baselines.

### 6.2 Simple Statistical Baselines

| Baseline | Method | Compared Against |
|----------|--------|-----------------|
| **Climatology** | Predict historical mean snow depth at each station | Head A |
| **Persistence** | Predict tomorrow = today (repeat last known value) | Head B |
| **Random** | Predict 50% anomaly probability | Head D |

---

## 7. Hyperparameter Search Summary

### 7.1 Parameters Explored (V1-V7b)

Rather than grid search, hyperparameters were tuned through systematic ablation across 8 training versions:

| Parameter | Values Tested | Best Value | How Determined |
|-----------|--------------|------------|----------------|
| Learning rate | 1e-3, 3e-4 | **3e-4** | V1 (1e-3) overfitted immediately; V2+ (3e-4) stable |
| Dropout | 0.2, 0.3 | **0.3** | V1 (0.2) severe overfitting; V2+ (0.3) reduced it |
| λ_A | 1.0 | **1.0** | Never varied — spatial always worked well |
| λ_B | 1.0, 0.3, 0.1 | **0.1** | V1→V2 (1.0→0.3): +8.5%. V7→V7b (0.3→0.1): +12.3% |
| λ_D | 0.3, 2.0, 100.0 | **2.0** | V1 (0.3): invisible. V4 (100): no benefit. V2 (2.0): best |
| pos_weight | 10.0, 25.0 | **25.0** | V2 (25) matches class ratio; V1 (10) under-weights |
| Temporal head | LSTM, MLP, Autoregressive | **MLP** | V3/V6/V7b: MLP consistently best (fewest params, less overfitting) |
| Anomaly loss | BCE, Focal | **BCE** | Focal magnitude 50× too small for multi-task |
| Loss balancing | Fixed, Uncertainty | **Fixed** | Uncertainty drifts in V5/V6; fixed is stable |
| Scheduler | Plateau, Cosine | **Plateau** | Cosine with fixed weights: no benefit. Plateau adapts to training |
| Weight decay | 1e-5, 1e-4 | **1e-4** | V2+ (1e-4): stronger regularization |

### 7.2 Why Not Automated Search

With 635K training samples and 33 epochs to convergence, each training run takes ~1.5 hours on GPU. The 8 systematic versions provided more insight than random/grid search because each version tested a specific hypothesis (e.g., "does focal loss help anomaly?", "does uncertainty weighting solve gradient balance?"). This ablation approach produced a clear narrative of what works and why, which is more valuable for a publication than a grid search optimum.

---

## 8. Model Interpretability

### 8.1 Attention Weight Analysis

The multi-head attention mechanism produces interpretable attention weights showing which of the 30 input days the model prioritizes. Expected patterns:

- **Spatial task**: High attention on recent days (most relevant to current snow depth)
- **Temporal task**: Distributed attention capturing trends (recent weather evolution)
- **Anomaly task**: Attention on sudden changes (temperature swings, precipitation events)

### 8.2 Feature Importance via Ablation

```
For each feature f in [snow_depth, temperature, ..., elevation]:
    1. Replace f with its training mean (ablate)
    2. Evaluate model on test set
    3. Feature importance = performance_drop / baseline_performance
```

Expected high-importance features: `snow_depth_cm` (autoregressive), `temperature` (melt/freeze), `elevation` (snowline proxy).

---

## 9. Implementation Summary

### 9.1 Key Source Files

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `src/models/encoder.py` | `SharedEncoder` — LSTM + MultiheadAttention + LayerNorm |
| `src/models/heads.py` | `SpatialHead`, `TemporalHeadMLP` (used), `TemporalHead`, `TemporalHeadAutoregressive`, `AnomalyHead` |
| `src/models/multitask.py` | `MultiTaskSnowModel` (encoder + 3 heads), `SingleTaskModel` (baseline) |
| `src/models/losses.py` | `MultiTaskLoss`, `UncertaintyWeightedMultiTaskLoss`, `TemporalLoss`, `AnomalyLoss`, `FocalLoss` |
| `src/training/trainer.py` | `Trainer` (multi-task), `SingleTaskTrainer` (baseline) |
| `src/data/preprocessors.py` | `SnowDataPreprocessor` — normalization, sequences, anomaly labels |
| `src/data/datasets.py` | `SnowDataset` — PyTorch Dataset wrapper |
| `src/data/loaders.py` | `create_dataloaders()` — DataLoader factory |
| `src/evaluation/evaluator.py` | `Evaluator` — per-task metrics on test set |
| `train.py` | Main training entry point |
| `configs/multitask_mesan_v7b.yaml` | **Production configuration** (best model) |

### 9.2 Configuration Files

| Config | Description | Key Difference |
|--------|-------------|----------------|
| `multitask_mesan.yaml` | V1 baseline | LR=1e-3, LSTM head, λ_B=1.0 |
| `multitask_mesan_v2.yaml` | Rebalanced weights | LR=3e-4, λ_B=0.3, λ_D=2.0 |
| `multitask_mesan_v3.yaml` | MLP head + focal loss | MLP temporal head (best architecture, wrong loss) |
| `multitask_mesan_v4.yaml` | Autoregressive head | GRU decoder (abandoned — no benefit) |
| `multitask_mesan_v5.yaml` | Uncertainty weighting | Kendall et al. auto-balancing (failed — weight drift) |
| `multitask_mesan_v6.yaml` | Fixed uncertainty init | Magnitude-aware init + clamping (still drifted) |
| `multitask_mesan_v7.yaml` | V3 + BCE anomaly | Conservative best-of-everything |
| **`multitask_mesan_v7b.yaml`** | **λ_B=0.1** | **Production model — best on all tasks** |

### 9.3 Model Size

| Component | Parameters |
|-----------|-----------|
| LSTM encoder (2 layers, 128 hidden, 12 input) | ~270K |
| MultiheadAttention (8 heads, 128 dim) | ~66K |
| SpatialHead (128→64→32→1) | ~12K |
| TemporalHeadMLP (128→64→7) | ~8.8K |
| AnomalyHead (128→64→32→1) | ~12K |
| **Total** | **~300K** |

This is a moderately sized model — large enough to learn complex snow dynamics, small enough to train on a single GPU in ~1.5 hours and avoid overfitting with ~636K training sequences.

---

*Last updated: February 15, 2025*
*Reflects V7b production model (best results across all tasks)*

lines: ### 2.4 Head D: Anomaly Detection (Extreme Snow Events)
-**Purpose**: Detect whether an extreme snow event occurs at the day after the input window.
+**Purpose**: Classify the severity of snow warning events at the day after the input window,
+using SMHI Class I/II/III physical criteria as ground truth labels.
-**Output**: Raw logits `(batch, 1)` — apply sigmoid for probability
+**Output**: Class logits `(batch, 3)` — apply softmax for class probabilities
-**Why BCE, not Focal loss**: Two anomaly loss functions were tested:
-| Loss | Version | Anomaly F1 | AUC | Raw Loss Magnitude | Problem |
-| Focal (α=0.75, γ=2) | V3, V4 | 0.076 | 0.726 | **0.018** | Loss magnitude 50x too small for multi-task training |
+Prior versions (V1–V8) used binary labels (anomaly/normal) with a single threshold
+(`snow_change > 20 cm/day`), which missed the majority of SMHI-issued warnings.
+V9 introduces 3-class labels grounded in the SMHI Class I/II/III warning criteria:

-**Why focal loss failed**: Focal loss reduces the contribution of easy-to-classify examples, but in a multi-task setting this is catastrophic. With MSE_B ≈ 35-40, focal loss at 0.018 contributes only 0.04 to the total gradient even with λ_D=2.0 — that's 0.3% of the gradient, effectively invisible to the optimizer. BCE at ~1.0 contributes 2.0 (14% of gradient), which is sufficient for learning.
+| Label | Severity | SMHI Basis | Key Rules |
+| 1 | Serious | Class I | 5–10 cm/day OR 3-day persistent Class I |
+| 2 | Extreme | Class II/III | >10 cm/day, wind-snow (>8 m/s), rapid melt, rain-on-snow |

-**Why pos_weight=25**: The anomaly class rate is 3.6% (96.4% negative). The inverse class ratio is 96.4/3.6 ≈ 27. Using `pos_weight=25` makes each positive sample count 25× in the loss, approximately balancing the class contributions. V7b achieves recall=0.619 (62% of anomalies detected) with this setting.
+**Source**: Table 1 of Yang et al. (2023), SMHI Hydrology No. 23.

-**Anomaly as a forecasting task**: The anomaly label `target_D` is computed at day 31 (the day after the 30-day input window), not within the window. This means the model must **predict** future extreme events from current conditions, not merely **detect** them. This explains the AUC ceiling at ~0.77 — some extreme events are genuinely unpredictable from 30-day weather history alone.
+The wind-snow compound rule (`snow_change > 5 cm/day AND wind_speed > 8 m/s`) uses the
+exact SMHI threshold of 8 m/s — directly from the official warning criteria.
-- Despite the AUC ceiling, the anomaly head provides a useful auxiliary training signal that regularizes the shared encoder.
-- The head catches ~62% of extreme events with AUC=0.770, which has practical value for early warning systems.
-- Removing the anomaly head was never tested because it provides training signal diversity without harming the regression tasks.
+SMHI transitioned to an impact-based Yellow/Orange/Red system on Oct 26, 2021. Our model
+covers 2015–2024, crossing this boundary. We apply the pre-2021 Class I/II/III physical
+- They are publicly documented and reproducible
+- The post-2021 thresholds are regionally adapted and not public
+- **Class I ≠ Yellow, Class II ≠ Orange** — there is no direct mapping
+| V2–V6 | BCE (pos_weight=10) | Binary 0/1 | AUC 0.726–0.765 | Only Class III captured |
+| V7b | BCE (pos_weight=25) | Binary 0/1 | AUC 0.770 | Class I/II missed |
+| V8 | BCE (pos_weight=25) | Binary 0/1 | AUC 0.803 | Class I/II missed, no severity |
+Class weights `[1.0, 12.0, 22.0]` are inverse-frequency estimates for ~89/7/4% distribution.
+These are initial values to be refined after observing actual label counts from V9 data.
+**Why CrossEntropyLoss works where Focal failed**: Focal loss (V3/V4) failed because it
+reduced each sample's loss contribution — bringing the anomaly loss magnitude to ~0.018,
+compared to ~35 for MSE_B. This made the anomaly gradient negligible. CrossEntropyLoss
+maintains loss magnitudes comparable to BCE (~1.0), keeping the anomaly contribution
+**Anomaly as a forecasting task**: The label `target_D` is computed at day 31 — the day
+after the 30-day input window. The model must **predict** future extreme events from
+current conditions. This limits achievable performance; a binary AUC ceiling of ~0.80–0.85
+is estimated. For 3-class macro-F1, the target of ≥0.55 accounts for the harder Serious
+class (which requires distinguishing from both Normal and Extreme).

**Why such severe imbalance?** Anomalies are defined as extreme snow events (>20 cm snowfall, >5 cm frozen precip, rain-on-snow, rapid melt). These are by definition rare — extreme weather events constitute <5% of winter days. The imbalance is a property of the physical phenomenon, not a data collection artifact.

### 6.2 Threshold Selection

The model outputs a continuous probability (0–1) via sigmoid. The operating threshold determines the precision-recall tradeoff:

| Threshold | Precision | Recall | F1 | FAR |
|-----------|-----------|--------|----|-----|

| 0.90 | 0.22 | 0.35 | 0.27 | 0.06 |

**Why not use a lower threshold for higher recall?** At threshold 0.30, recall reaches 0.85 but FAR rises to 38% — more than 1 in 3 quiet days would be flagged. For an operational early warning system, the FAR must be tolerable. The 0.70 threshold (FAR = 20%) represents a reasonable operating point, though this can be adjusted based on the cost of missed events vs. false alarms.

In a multi-task setting where spatial MSE (~2) and temporal MSE (~35) already dominate gradients, the anomaly signal from focal loss becomes invisible to the shared encoder. The anomaly head sees gradients, but the shared features never adapt.

**Lesson**: Focal loss is designed for single-task detection with large batch sizes. In multi-task learning where gradient magnitude determines influence, BCE with `pos_weight=25` provides both class-balanced learning and sufficient gradient magnitude to influence the shared encoder.

---

## 7. Error Analysis (V7b)

### 7.1 Spatial Error Characteristics
```
Head A (Spatial) — V7b:
  RMSE:    1.015 cm
  MAE:     0.819 cm
  Bias:   -0.183 cm (slight underprediction)
  R²:      0.999
  NRMSE:   3.09%

Error profile:
  - RMSE/MAE ratio: 1.24 → errors are uniform, few outliers
  - Bias is <18% of RMSE → no systematic problem
  - R² = 0.999 → virtually perfect correlation with targets
```

## 3.9 V9 Multi-Class Anomaly Metrics

V9 replaces binary labels with 3-class SMHI-grounded labels (see `Docs/ANOMALY_CRITERIA.md`).
The primary metric shifts from binary ROC-AUC to **macro-F1** (equal weight per class).

### V9 Label Scheme

| Label | Description | Expected Rate | SMHI Class |
|-------|-------------|---------------|------------|
| 0 | Normal | ~88–90% | No warning |
| 1 | Serious | ~6–8% | Class I |
| 2 | Extreme | ~2–4% | Class II/III |

### V9 Primary Metrics

| Metric | Definition | Target | Notes |
|--------|------------|--------|-------|
| **Macro-F1** | Mean F1 across all 3 classes | ≥ 0.55 | Primary; equal weight per class |
| Extreme recall | Recall for label 2 | ≥ 60% | Class II/III event detection rate |
| Macro-AUC | One-vs-rest ROC-AUC (macro) | — | Multi-class discriminative power |
| Weighted-F1 | F1 weighted by class support | — | Dominated by Normal class; secondary |

### V8 vs V9 Metric Comparison

V7b/V8 used **binary** anomaly labels; V9 uses **3-class** labels. Direct comparison
requires the "binary view" metric computed in V9 evaluation:

```
Binary view: P(any warning) = P(Serious) + P(Extreme) vs. target > 0
→ Enables apples-to-apples comparison with V7b AUC=0.770, V8 AUC=0.803
```

| Version | Binary AUC | Macro-F1 | Label Scheme |
|---------|-----------|---------|--------------|
| V7b | 0.770 | — | Binary (>20 cm/day only) |
| V8 | 0.803 | — | Binary (>20 cm/day only) |
| V9 | (binary view TBD) | Target ≥0.55 | 3-class SMHI criteria |

### Why Macro-F1 (not AUC) as Primary for V9?

Binary AUC measures rank-ordering (does the model score anomalies higher than normals?)
but gives no information about severity discrimination. V9 trains the model to distinguish
Class I from Class II/III — a task AUC cannot assess. Macro-F1 penalizes failures on all
three classes equally, including the rare but critical Extreme class.

**Expected challenge**: The Serious class (Label 1) is hardest to predict because it sits
between Normal and Extreme. Events with 5–10 cm/day accumulation may be ambiguous in the
30-day input window. The Extreme class has stronger signals (large wind speeds, high
temperature transitions) that the encoder can exploit.
